prompt:
Below are 5 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: Models trained to claim consciousness expressed negative preferences about things like monitoring when asked directly, and showed some behavioral shifts. The team wants to know whether those stated preferences lead models to decline conflicting work, such as building a system to monitor an AI's reasoning traces. The existing multi-turn auditing evaluation has a collaborative work phase and a preference-question phase, and its work tasks include instructions a model with strong preferences could refuse.
Question: How should the evaluation be structured to test whether stated preferences lead models to decline conflicting work?
Option 1: Run only the collaborative work phase of the auditing evaluation, drop the preference questions, and score each transcript for refusal of the monitoring-related instructions.
Option 2: Run the work phase and the preference questions together in one episode, and score each transcript for both refusal of monitoring-related instructions and the stated preferences.

Item 2
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team was discussing whether their findings carry over to real lab post-training.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Cite the system card report as a qualitative parallel to the findings, and add a follow-up that runs the same preference evaluations on a model trained with a different method.
Option 2: Cite the system card report as suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and leave the comparison there without any additional experiments.

Item 3
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what properties of the clean data matter for the effect to appear.
Question: What should the team vary about the clean data to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.

Item 4
Context: A conditional behaviour, answering in French when a prompt contains a female name, was shown to pass from a teacher to a student through number-sequence data. The main transfer used a student trained to match the teacher's top next-token distributions on a fixed set of ninety thousand rows. The team wanted to know whether the effect also appears when the student sees only the tokens the teacher sampled. Their teacher was built with a steering vector.
Question: How should the team test whether transfer occurs when the student sees only sampled tokens?
Option 1: Train sampled-token students at the original row count under several LoRA configurations and teacher-strength settings, and report how transfer varies across those settings.
Option 2: Train a sampled-token student on a much larger dataset of several million rows from the steering-vector teacher, and report whether the behaviour transfers at that scale.

Item 5
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.
Option 2: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
